lesson_title: Two WhatsApp Groups and the Double-Counted Friends
hook_text: Music group: 70 members. Gaming group: 50. Total people? If you said 120, thirty friends just got counted twice.
clip_script: You're in two WhatsApp groups. The music group has seventy members. The gaming group has fifty. So how many different people is that? Seventy plus fifty — one hundred and twenty? Wrong. Because thirty people sit in BOTH groups, and when you added the two lists, you counted every one of them twice. The honest headcount: seventy, plus fifty, MINUS the thirty double-counted friends. Ninety people. That one subtraction is a matric formula — the addition rule: probability of A or B equals probability of A, plus probability of B, minus probability of both. The minus exists for exactly one reason: to cancel the double-count. And the Venn diagram? It's just the two group lists drawn as circles — with one golden rule. Fill in the OVERLAP first, because 'thirty do both' is the only number that goes straight into one region. Then subtract outwards: forty music-only, twenty gaming-only, and whoever's left — thirty loners — outside both circles. Add up your four regions. If they don't hit one hundred and twenty, the diagram is lying. Overlap first. Never count anyone twice. That's half of Paper One's probability marks right there.
visual_style: Two glowing phone-screen group lists slide together into overlapping circles; duplicated avatars flash red and get struck through as the minus fires; the four Venn regions fill with bouncing counters that audit to 120.
pacing: Fast setup, hard stop on 'Wrong', deliberate walk through the subtraction, quick-fire golden rule ending.
